questions.question: How would you explain the transition from private collections to public museums? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• How would you explain the transition from private collections to publicmuseums? Private
  • collections of rulers, aristocrats and scholars gradually became public museums through the
  • Enlightenment, political revolutions and educational reforms. Collections were transferred to
  • public institutions, systematically classified and opened to wider audiences. This transition
  • changed their p urpose from displaying wealth and prestige to promoting public education,
  • research and heritage preservation.

questions.question: Remedial Preservation / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Remedial Preservation Remedial preservation involves direct action on museum objects
  • to arrest deterioration and stabilise their condition. Unl ike preventive preservation, which
  • controls environmental risks, it addresses existing damage. Measures include treating insect
  • infestations, stabilising corroding metals and consolidating fragile materials. Such
  • interventions require trained professionals, appropriate materials, careful documentation and
  • minimal alteration.

questions.solution_html:

  • include archaeological, art, maritime, science and textile museums. Such museums provide
  • focused knowledge and support specialised research and education.

  • to acquire historically, artistically or scientifically significant materials, often without purchase
  • costs. Museums accept bequests after assessing their relevance, legal ownership,
  • associated conditions and requirements for future care.

questions.question: Analyse the major differences between traditional museology and New Museology. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the major differences between traditional museology and NewMuseology. ?
  • Traditional museology centres on objects, collections and institutional authority ,
  • emphasising acquisition, classification, conservation, research and display. Experts
  • generally determine interpretation, while visitors mainly receive information. Museums often
  • present established historical narratives within dedicated buildings. New Museology shifts
  • emphasis towards people, communities and social relevance . It promotes participation,
  • shared authority, inclusive interpretation and recognition of diverse identities. Collections are
  • understood through their social contexts, including power, inequality and colonialism.
  • Ecomuseums and community museums illustrate its broader approach to heritage. Thus, the
  • major differences concern object versus community orientation, expert versus shared
  • authority, and preservation versus wider social engagement , while retaining
  • conservation.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Analyse the problems that may arise when museum documentation is incomplete. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the problems that may arise when museum documentation
  • isincomplete.Incomplete museum documentation creates uncertainty about an object’s
  • identity, provenance, ownership and significance. Missing acquisition records can cause
  • legal disputes and ethical concerns , especially regarding stolen or illicitly traded
  • antiquities. Inadequate location records increase the risk of misplacement, theft and loss,
  • while missing condition reports hinder conservation planning and damage assessment.
  • Researchers may draw incorrect conclusions, and exhibitions may communicate misleading
  • interpretations. Poor documentation also obstructs loans, insurance claims, audits and
  • repatriation requests. Consequently, incomplete records weaken collection management,
  • institutional accountability and public trust , reducing the museum’s ability to preserve
  • objects, support research and communicate reliable knowledge to future generations.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the importance of budgeting and financial records in museums. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of budgeting and financial records in museums. Budgeting and
  • financial records are essential for responsible museum management. Budgeting estimates
  • income and expenditure, establishes priorities and allocates resources for collections,
  • conservation, exhibitions, staffing, security and visitor services . It helps museums
  • control costs, anticipate shortages and plan future development. Financial records document
  • receipts, payments, grants and purchases, providing evidence of h ow funds are used.
  • Accurate records support auditing, legal compliance and accountability , while helping
  • prevent fraud and financial mismanagement. They also enable comparison between planned
  • and actual expenditure. Together, budgeting and financial docume ntation strengthen
  • transparency, donor confidence and financial sustainability , enabling museums to fulfil
  • their educational and cultural responsibilities.

questions.question: Explain why the legal definition of antiquity is important in controlling the movement of cultural objects. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain why the legal definition of antiquity is important in controlling themovement of
  • cultural objects ? The legal definition of antiquity establishes which cultural objects fall
  • under statutory protection, using criteria such as age, historical significance and object
  • category. It provides a basis for regulating their sale, transfer, import and ex port. Clear
  • definitions help authorities identify protected objects, require appropriate documentation and
  • permissions, and distinguish lawful transactions from illicit trafficking. They also guide
  • museums, collectors and dealers in checking provenance and ownership before acquisition.
  • Without clear definitions, ambiguity can enable illegal movement and weaken enforcement.
  • Thus, legal definitions support consistent enforcement, accountability and heritage
  • protection, while facilitating the lawful movement of cultural objects for legitimate purposes.

questions.question: Compare the institutional objectives and collection profiles of the Indian Museum, Kolkata and the National Museum, New Delhi. / [CO1]

• Compare the institutional objectives and collection profiles of the IndianMuseum, Kolkata
  • and the National Museum, New Delhi ? The Indian Museum, Kolkata, established in 1814,

  • heritage. Its collections encompass archaeology, art, anthropology, zoology, geology
  • and botany, supporting scientific study and public education. Indian Museum Kolkata The
  • National Museum, New Delhi , established in 1949, primarily presents India’s cultural
  • heritage and historical development . Its collections include Harappan antiquities,
  • sculptures, paintin gs, manuscripts, coins, textiles, decorative arts and arms . Both
  • institutions promote conservation, research and education. Their principal distinction lies in
  • collection scope: the Indian Museum combines natural history and human culture , while
  • the Nation al Museum concentrates on art, archaeology and the diversity of Indian
  • civilisation.

questions.question: Analyse how the geographical and subject limits of a collection policy help a museum maintain a focused collection. / [CO2]

• Analyse how the geographical and subject limits of a collection policyhelp a museum
  • maintain a focused collection ? Geographical and subject limits define the scope of a
  • museum’s collection policy. Geographical limits specify the regions represented, while
  • subject limits identify relevant themes, disciplines or object categories. Together, they guide
  • acquisition decisions, ensuring that objects suppo rt the museum’s mission. They prevent
  • indiscriminate collecting, unnecessary duplication and the acceptance of unsuitable
  • donations. A focused collection allows limited funds, storage and professional expertise
  • to be used effectively. These boundaries also strengthen research, coherent exhibitions and
  • meaningful interpretation. Periodic review allows justified changes while maintaining
  • institutional purpose. Thus, clearly defined limits promote collection relevance,
  • responsible growth and effective management over the long term.

• Explain how documentation supports the enforcement of the Antiquitiesand Art Treasures
  • Act? Documentation supports enforcement of the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act,

  • them from replicas. Registration records, provenance details and transaction

• Assess the significance of specialised museums in preserving specificaspects of Kerala’s
  • cultural and natural herita ge.Specialised museums preserve selected aspects of Kerala’s
  • heritage through focused collection, conservation, research and interpretation. Museums
  • devoted to folklore, maritime traditions, archaeology, traditional crafts and biodiversity

  • document local skills, community histories and environmental diversity, supporting education
  • and specialised research. By involving practitioners and communities, they strengthen
  • cultural continuity and regional identity. Natural history collections also provide evidence
  • for understanding ecological change. However, their effectiveness depends on adequate
  • funding, professional care and inclusive interpretation. Their significance lies i n preserving
  • distinctive heritage within its wider social, historical and environmental contexts
  • meaningfully.

questions.question: Trace the origin and historical evolution of the term museum and discuss its changing meaning / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Trace the origin and historical evolution of the term museum anddiscuss its changing
  • meaning? The term museum derives from the Greek mouseion, meaning a place dedicated
  • to the Muses, the goddesses of arts and learning. In antiquity, it referred to a centre of
  • intellectual activity rather than a modern exhibition institution. The Mouseion of Alexandria
  • exemplified this association with scholarship and research. During the Renaissance, the
  • term became associated with collections of antiquities, artworks and natural specimens
  • assembled by rulers and scholars. Cabinets of curiosities reflected interests in collecting,
  • classification and discovery. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries , public
  • museums expanded, transforming private collections into institutions serving education,
  • research and national identity . In the twentieth century, conservation, profession al
  • management and public interpretation became increasingly important. New Museology
  • subsequently emphasised communities, participation and social responsibility. Today, the
  • museum is understood as an institution serving society through heritage preservati on,
  • accessibility, inclusion and learning , reflecting a shift from exclusive scholarly spaces
  • towards public engagement and shared cultural understanding.

questions.question: Describe the main causes of deterioration of non-biological museum objects and explain the importance of preventive care. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the main causes of deterioration of non -biological museumobjects and explain
  • the importa nce of preventive care ? Non-biological museum objects , including metals,
  • stone, ceramics and glass, deteriorate through physical, chemical and environmental
  • processes. Excessive or fluctuating relative humidity encourages metal corrosion, salt
  • crystallisation and instability in certain glasses. Temperature changes can cause expansion,
  • contraction and cracking, particularly in composite objects. Air pollutants, dust and
  • soluble salts promote surface damage, staining and chemical reactions. Light can fade
  • pigments and painted decoration, while heat may damage associated materials. Improper
  • handling, vibration, impact and unsuitable storage cause breakage, abrasion and
  • deformation. Earlier repairs using incompatible materials may introduce further deterioration.
  • Preventive care reduces these risks before damage occurs through environmental
  • monitoring, suitable storage, protective enclosures, careful handling, regular inspection and
  • emergency planning. Stable conditions and appropriate supports help preserve stru ctural
  • integrity and surface details. Preventive care is important because it minimises irreversible
  • damage, reduces the need for remedial treatment, lowers long -term costs and
  • preserves the evidential and cultural value of collections.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between curatorial work, research and exhibition planning. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the rel ationship between curatorial work, research andexhibition planning ?
  • Curatorial work, research and exhibition planning are interconnected museum functions
  • that transform collections into meaningful public knowledge. Curatorial work involves
  • selecting, documenting, interpreting and caring for objects, establishing the foundation for
  • their use. Research investigates their provenance, chronology, materials, functions and
  • cultural significance, while identifying gaps and questioning earlier interpretations. Thes e
  • findings guide exhibition planning, including the central theme, object selection, narrative
  • sequence, labels and supporting media. Curators collaborate with conservators, educators,
  • designers and communities to ensure that displays are accurate, accessible and sensitive to
  • cultural contexts. Conservation assessments determine whether objects can safely be
  • exhibited and under what conditions. Exhibition development may generate new research
  • questions, while visitor feedback can reveal weaknesses in interp retation. Thus, their
  • relationship is continuous and reciprocal : curatorial practice safeguards and organises
  • evidence, research develops understanding, and exhibitions communicate that
  • understanding. Together, they support responsible interpretation, publ ic education and
  • the museum’s wider social and scholarly purposes.

questions.question: Describe the main elements included in the legal definition of an archaeological site. / [CO5] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the main elements included in the legal definition of anarchaeological site. Give
  • a general introduction about acts and their importance then write about act of 1958. Under
  • Section 2(d) of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act,
  • 1958, an “archaeological site and remains” is an area containing, or reasonably believed
  • to contain, ruins or relics of historical or archaeological importance. The definition includes
  • several essential elements. First, it concerns a geographical area , rather than only an
  • individual object or standing structure. Second, the area must contain archaeological
  • evidence, or there must be reasonable grounds for believing that such evi dence exists,
  • allowing recognition before complete excavation. Third, the ruins or relics must possess
  • historical or archaeological importance and have existed for at least one hundred
  • years. Fourth, the definition includes adjoining land needed for fencin g, covering or
  • otherwise preserving the area. Finally, it encompasses means of access and convenient
  • inspection. These elements recognise that archaeological heritage includes remains, their
  • surrounding protective space and necessary access. However, class ification under this
  • definition does not automatically confer protected status.
